What does the PHP request lifecycle look like with Nginx and php-fpm?

Nginx serves static files itself and passes .php requests over FastCGI to a php-fpm pool. A free worker loads the script, which OPcache usually already has in compiled form, runs the bootstrap and autoloader, handles the request and returns the response. Then all request memory is freed. That is the shared-nothing model: nothing survives to the next request except what you store in sessions, a cache or the DB. 💡 When the site gets slow, check pm.max_children and the php-fpm slow log before blaming the code.
What does declare(strict_types=1) do?

It turns off scalar type coercion for function calls made from the file that declares it. Passing "5" to an int parameter then throws TypeError instead of silently converting. It must be the first statement in the file and applies per file, not to the whole project. Return types are checked in strict mode too. 💡 Put it in every new file and enforce it with PHP-CS-Fixer or PHPStan.
Difference between == and ===?

== compares after type juggling. === also requires the same type. PHP 8 made string-to-number comparison saner (0 == "a" is now false), but "1" == "01" and null == false are still true. Use ===, and pass true to in_array()/array_search() for strict checks.
How are PHP arrays different from Java collections?

A PHP array is one ordered hash map that works as a list, map, stack or queue. Keys are int or string, and insertion order is kept. Arrays are passed by value with copy-on-write, so a function that changes an array changes a copy unless the parameter is declared by reference &$arr. Java has separate List/Map/Set types passed by reference. For a typed, mutable collection in PHP you would use a small class or ArrayObject/SPL structures.
Interface vs abstract class vs trait?

An interface is a pure contract, and a class can implement many. An abstract class shares state and partial implementation and allows single inheritance only. A trait is reusable code copied into classes with use. It can hold properties and methods but is not a type, so you cannot type-hint a trait. Typical design: type-hint against interfaces, put shared base behavior in an abstract class, and use traits for small cross-cutting helpers such as timestamps or logging.
What is the difference between self::, static:: and parent::?

self:: resolves to the class where the code is written. static:: uses late static binding and resolves to the class that was actually called, which is what makes return new static() factories work in subclasses. parent:: calls the parent class's implementation, for example parent::__construct().
Explain PSR-4 autoloading and Composer.

Composer reads composer.json, resolves dependency versions, writes composer.lock and generates vendor/autoload.php. With PSR-4, a namespace prefix maps to a folder ("App\\": "src/"), so App\Billing\Invoice loads src/Billing/Invoice.php the first time it is used. That removes manual require calls. 💡 In CI and Docker builds run composer install --no-dev --optimize-autoloader against the committed lock file.

What are property hooks and asymmetric visibility in PHP 8.4?

Property hooks let a property declare its own get and/or set logic, so you can validate or normalize on write, or compute a virtual property, without writing getter and setter methods. Asymmetric visibility sets read and write scope separately, e.g. public private(set) string $id is publicly readable but only writable inside the class. Together they replace a lot of getter/setter boilerplate, similar to what Kotlin or C# properties give you on the JVM/.NET side.
readonly property vs readonly class vs constant?

A readonly property (8.1) can be set once, from inside the class scope (usually in the constructor). After that, any write throws Error. A readonly class (8.2) makes every declared property readonly and forbids dynamic properties. A class const is a compile-time value shared by all instances, and since 8.3 it can be typed. Note that readonly is shallow: an object stored in a readonly property can still change internally.
Exception vs Error in PHP?

Both implement Throwable. Exception is for recoverable application failures that your code throws and catches. Error comes from the engine: TypeError, ValueError, calling an undefined method, and so on. catch (Exception $e) does not catch an Error, so a top-level handler should catch Throwable. PHP has no checked exceptions; document thrown types with @throws.

How do you prevent XSS and CSRF?

XSS: escape output for its context. That means HTML body, HTML attribute, JavaScript and URL each need their own escaping. Use htmlspecialchars(..., ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8') or a template engine with autoescape such as Twig, avoid |raw, and add a CSP header. CSRF: give each session a random token, embed it in forms and AJAX headers, and verify it with hash_equals() on every state-changing request. SameSite cookies add a second layer of protection.
How should passwords be stored?

Store them with password_hash($password, PASSWORD_DEFAULT) and check them with password_verify(). This gives a salted, slow hash (bcrypt by default, Argon2id available) with the algorithm and cost stored inside the hash string. Call password_needs_rehash() at login to upgrade old hashes. Never use md5/sha1, never write your own salting scheme, and never log passwords.
How do sessions work and how do you secure them?

session_start() reads or creates a session ID that travels in a cookie, and the data stays on the server in $_SESSION. To secure them, set cookie flags (Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite), enable session.use_strict_mode, call session_regenerate_id(true) on login and privilege change, add idle and absolute timeouts, and fully destroy the session on logout. When running several containers, use a shared session store such as Redis or the DB.
Explain Twig template inheritance and autoescaping.

A base layout defines {% block %} placeholders. A child uses {% extends 'base.html.twig' %}, overrides only the blocks it needs and can call {{ parent() }} to keep the original content. {% include %} and {% embed %} reuse partials, and macros act like template functions. Autoescape is on by default with the HTML strategy, so every {{ }} output is escaped. You can switch strategy per value (|e('js'), |e('url')) or skip escaping with |raw for trusted content only.
How is PHP different from Java for building web apps?

PHP rebuilds the app on every request and scales by adding processes. Java keeps a long-running JVM where singletons, caches and connection pools live in memory. PHP's types are optional and checked at runtime, while Java's are static and checked at compile time. The concepts map closely: Composer↔Maven, Symfony/Laravel↔Spring, PHPUnit↔JUnit, Doctrine↔Hibernate, Twig↔Thymeleaf. 💡 Mention that static analysis (PHPStan/Psalm at a high level) gives PHP code much of the safety you get from the Java compiler.
isset vs empty vs is_null vs ??

isset($x) is true if the variable exists and is not null; it doesn't warn on undefined variables or array keys. empty($x) is true for missing or "falsy" values: null, false, 0, "0", "", [] — so "0" being empty is a classic bug. is_null($x) is true only for null and warns if undefined. $a ?? 'default' uses the default when the left side is unset or null, and ??= assigns only if null.
Closure vs arrow function in PHP?

A closure (function () use ($x) { … }) must list captured variables explicitly with use, by value or by reference (use (&$x)), and can have multiple statements. An arrow function (fn($p) => $p * $rate, PHP 7.4+) captures the outer scope automatically by value and is a single expression — similar to a Java lambda. Since 8.1 the first-class callable syntax strlen(...) creates a closure from any function or method.
What are generators and when would you use them?

A function containing yield returns a Generator that produces values lazily as you iterate. Memory stays constant, so it's ideal for reading big CSVs, paging through DB results or streaming exports. Generators can also receive values (send()), return a final value (getReturn()) and delegate with yield from. They're single-pass, like a Java Iterator.
Are PHP objects and arrays passed by value or by reference?

Arrays are passed by value but with copy-on-write: no copy happens until the function modifies it. Objects are passed as handles (like Java references), so a function can change the object's state but reassigning the parameter doesn't affect the caller. Use &$param for real references — sparingly, and beware the classic bug of a foreach ($arr as &$v) reference left alive after the loop (call unset($v)).
How do you handle file uploads securely?

Check $_FILES[...]['error'] and size, detect the real MIME type with finfo (not the client-supplied type or extension), allow-list types, generate a random file name, and store it outside the web root (or in object storage) with move_uploaded_file. Serve files through a controller that checks authorisation, with Content-Disposition and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff. Also set upload_max_filesize/post_max_size, and scan for malware if users share files.
Why is unserialize() on user input dangerous?

unserialize can create objects of any loaded class and then calls magic methods like __wakeup, __destruct or __toString on them. An attacker can chain existing classes ("gadget chains") to delete files or execute code — PHP object injection, the same class of bug as Java deserialisation vulnerabilities. Use JSON for data exchange, or pass ['allowed_classes' => false], and sign any serialized data you must store client-side.
What does __invoke do and where is it useful?

__invoke lets an object be called like a function ($handler($request)) and makes it a valid callable. It is common for single-action controllers, middleware and command handlers, where the class holds injected dependencies and the call does the work. It's similar to implementing a Java functional interface such as Function.
How do you work with UTF-8 strings correctly in PHP?

Core string functions (strlen, substr, strtoupper) work on bytes, so they break on multibyte characters such as Tamil, Hindi or emoji. Use the mbstring functions (mb_strlen, mb_substr, mb_strtoupper), set the DB connection charset to utf8mb4 (PDO DSN charset=utf8mb4), and send Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8. htmlspecialchars defaults to UTF-8 in PHP 8.
How do you unit test PHP code?

With PHPUnit (or Pest on top of it): test classes extend TestCase, use assertions such as assertSame, data providers for parameterised cases, and test doubles via createMock() (Mockery is an alternative). Write code with constructor injection so dependencies can be replaced, use an in-memory or containerised database for repository tests, and run PHPStan/Psalm static analysis in CI alongside the tests. Xdebug or PCOV provides code coverage.
